== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## The specification and the repository's lineage

FACTS.md:177
- **The team's latest word on types and on the exclusion rule is the unfinished restart, not `Specification/`** (`coordinator/spec-lineage.md` and its coordinator's check): `Documentation/Specification/` was begun 2012-02-20 (Luchangco, `166841592`) and abandoned 2012-05-31 with a 65-page build and mostly skeleton chapters; it was never adopted. Its Types chapter (`Prose/Language/types.tick`, Luchangco, 2012-05-31, `275b90773`) is from-scratch prose written a year and a half after `Specification/`'s last edit. It restates the rule as "instantiation exclusion" (:353-376), with a `\note` giving the stronger imposed form: a trait extending two instantiations must extend an expressible one below both. It adds a `covariant` modifier on trait static parameters (:320-339), where the older draft expresses covariance with a self-extending `where` clause (`trait-parameters.tex:339-352`). And it says `Bottom` is inexpressible (:173-195). On static parameters, traits, exceptions, components and the numeric library, `Specification/` is the only statement. "July 19, 2012" on our PDF is the date of the parentless import `5a68404fd`, chosen by the revival in `414b790e3`, not a date of any edit. `fortress.1.0.pdf` is the team's own 2008 artefact (`403afbe0b`), and the root `README.md:106-108` calls the directory beside it "the frozen Fortress 1.0 specification", which only the PDF is. Later than both is the type group's last published word on instantiation and dispatch: Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, "Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance", PACMPL 3, POPL 2019, Article 11 (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`, read from the full text; the review of Pavol's decisions rechecked against it, `reviews/decisions-review/popl-recheck.md`). At run-time dispatch a type parameter that nothing fixes takes the intersection of its upper bounds, its declared bound and the constraint of the call's static return type, and the solver never instantiates it at `Bottom` (p. 11:19); the team's earlier assumption, the union of the lower bounds, the authors could not prove (p. 11:25). Of static inference the paper asks only that it instantiate at non-`Bottom` types (pp. 11:16-17), gives no algorithm (p. 11:25), and annotates its one static example, `O.m(3, true)`, at the union `Int ⊔ Boolean` (p. 11:21). The run-time check of the return type chooses the instance, never the declaration (Lemmas 5.8 and 5.9, pp. 11:22-23): Naden's second write-up's proposal (`Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/RTRinstantionTheory.tex:73-80`), not the static context limiting which declarations apply, which his first rejected (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex:241-305`). A type parameter's default bounds are `Any` and `Bottom` (p. 11:9). No method type parameter may appear in an upper bound (p. 11:11), so the paper's soundness theorem does not cover the library's F-bounded functions, `SUM`, `BIG MAX` and those over `Integral[\I\]`. Theorem 4.1 keeps static uniqueness, a unique most specific declaration for every call (p. 11:15); the exclusion rule is [Anc-Same-Trait], a class that extends two instances of a trait extends an instance below both (p. 11:11), blanket for an invariant parameter; and [D-Method] keeps a covariant parameter out of parameter positions, so no self-typed algebra trait can be covariant (`Equality[\+T\]`; the recheck's § 1.1). It has no closed types, nominal exclusion, modules or top-level functions (pp. 11:3, 11:25), and no coercion or numbers. The paper is CC BY-NC 4.0; its PDF and its text stay in the gitignored `research/decks/`. Its instance rule is Pavol's decision (POSITIONS, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`"), and the checker's `Bottom` binding it replaces is "Keeping the expected type at a call written `f(x)` ..." under The checker and the one library.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record

POSITIONS.md:26
- **The type group's late positions outweigh the early text.** The specification "was written in a vacuum early on", "as a wish"; "then the type group went in and tried to make it run. So they knew much more about what's feasible and what's not. The goal was performance. The specialization is a must"; "when that wish met reality, then the spec must change"; "whatever the spec was dreaming about in 2008 is irrelevant because it met hard reality". So the late, implementation-informed positions of the type group (the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the compiled tower flattened by Steele in 2011, Naden's 2012 write-up, the POPL 2019 paper) outweigh the specification's earlier text where they conflict, and the implementers' later word outweighs unfinished text. "We are not Naden. We know nothing here."

1	# Extract: Guy L. Steele Jr., "Fortress Features and Lessons Learned" (JuliaCon 2016)
     2	
     3	Working notes on the recovered PDF (`research/decks/SteeleJuliaCon2016.pdf`,
     4	49 slides, © 2016 Oracle — personal copy only, the PDF itself is gitignored and
     5	never committed). These notes are our own summary and commentary with brief
     6	attributed quotations, not a reproduction of the deck.
     7	Source: Oracle Labs APEX DOC_ID:952, recovered via Wayback; video:
     8	https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EZD3Scuv02g
     9	
    10	Extract made 2026-08-18 from a full read of all 49 slides. Slide numbers are the
    11	printed page numbers. Cross-references to the palimondo/fortress repo state are
    12	marked **[repo]**.
    13	
    14	## 1–3. Front matter
    15	
    16	Title (2): "Fortress Features and Lessons Learned", Guy L. Steele Jr., Software
    17	Architect, Oracle Labs. Slide 3: copyright notice — personal/classroom copies
    18	permitted, no redistribution without written permission of Oracle.
    19	
    20	## 4–9. The toy problem: histogram water
    21	
    22	Array of bar heights `2 6 3 5 2 8 1 4 2 2 5 3 5 7 4 1`; rain fills valleys; how
    23	much water is retained? (Thanks to Dan Nussbaum and Steve Heller.) Key insight
    24	(7–8): water level above each bar = `(max-to-the-left MIN max-to-the-right) − v`.
    25	
    26	Slide 9 — the concise Fortress solution (typeset with ∑, highlighted parts):
    27	
    28	```
    29	histogramWater(x: List[\ZZ32\]): ZZ32 =
    30	  SUM [(v,left,right) <- zip(x, MAX-prefix x, MAX-suffix x)]
    31	      ((left MIN right) - v)
    32	```
    33	
    34	(The typeset original zips `x` with a forward running `MAX` and a backward
    35	running `MAX`, drawn as arrows over `MAX x`.) Notes: purely functional; allows
    36	map-reduce parallelism. Pointer to Google Tech Talk "Four Solutions to a Trivial
    37	Problem" on YouTube.
    38	
    39	## 10–17. Principles
    40	
    41	- Slide 10 — **Three principles**: a growable language, a mathematical language,
    42	  a parallel language. "We tried very hard to avoid including any language
    43	  feature not clearly justified by one or more of these principles."
    44	- Slide 11 — Growability: modular libraries (components and APIs, separate
    45	  compilation, multiple co-existing implementations of one interface); break
    46	  with Fortran's array emphasis — objects with *multiple inheritance* of traits
    47	  ("Why inheritance? Sharing of code. Why multiple? Even more sharing of
    48	  code."); distributed/hierarchical arrays; therefore *multimethods*
    49	  (type-directed dispatch on multiple arguments).
    50	- Slide 12 — Paradigmatic examples: extensible numeric hierarchy — multiple-size
    51	  ints/floats incl. big, **"Rational, complex, and quaternion"**, interval
    52	  arithmetic; vectors/matrices/tensors (matrix-vector both ways); collections;
    53	  arrays (multidimensional, distributed, sparse). Goal: multiple implementations
    54	  of the same interface coexisting in one program. **[repo]** Only rational
    55	  shipped; this is the never-kept promise behind the §4d complex-numbers roadmap
    56	  (seed: `complex_ring.fss` runs on the interpreter).
    57	- Slide 13 — Operator overloading included: mathematical tradition; bad
    58	  experience with Java's BigInteger/BigDecimal; contrast Gosling's C++ trauma.
    59	- Slide 14 — Growability requires reliability: strong types; type AND method
    60	  parameters may be types, operator names, integers, booleans, physical
    61	  dimensions/units; design-by-contract (pre/post-conditions, inheritable
    62	  invariants); rich library of algebraic traits:
    63	  `trait ZZ extends { Ring[\ZZ,+,x\], PartialOrder[\ZZ,<,<=,>=,>\] } ... end`
    64	  **[repo]** Spec-fiction: no operator-parameterized `Ring` ever shipped — the
    65	  implementation has operator-fixed `AdditiveGroup`/`MultiplicativeRing`.
    66	- Slide 15 — Algebraic traits (with the F-bounded self-type pattern and `opr ⊙`
    67	  operator parameters):
    68	  `trait BinaryOperator[\T extends BinaryOperator[\T,⊙\], opr ⊙\]`
    69	  with `opr ⊙(self, other:T):T`; `Associative` and `Commutative` extend
    70	  {BinaryOperator, EquivalenceRelation} and carry `property ∀(a,b,c:T)`
    71	  associativity/commutativity laws. "Properties can be checked by unit testing.
    72	  (Future work: theorem prover.)" **[repo]** `property` keyword never shipped.
    73	- Slide 16 — Big example: `trait BooleanAlgebra[\T ..., opr ∧, opr ∨, opr ∼,
    74	  opr ⊕, ident zero, ident one\]` extending Commutative/Associative/Idempotent
    75	  (×2), HasIdentity (×2), Complements (×2), Distributive (×2), DeMorgan (×2),
    76	  and `Ring[\T,⊕,IDENTITY,∧,zero,one\]`; one property `∼(∼a)=a`; `opr ⊕`
    77	  defined by default in terms of ∧, ∨, ∼.
    78	- Slide 17 — **Fourth principle: symmetry.** Order should not matter:
    79	  declarations in a file, imports, declared parents, overload resolution,
    80	  argument evaluation. Order *does* matter for: matching args to params, tuple
    81	  construction, statement execution in a block.
    82	
    83	## 18–21. Fortress vs Scala
    84	
    85	- Slide 18 — histogramWater via `maxCachedTree`/`walk` over Pair/Leaf in both
    86	  languages; Fortress `walk(x.a, left, x.b.val MAX right) + walk(x.b, left MAX
    87	  x.a.val, right)` is *potentially parallel recursion*; the Scala twin is
    88	  sequential.
    89	- Slide 19 — Typeset vs ASCII Fortress: same walk code as
    90	  `histogramWater(x: List[\ZZ\]): ZZ`, `(*) comment`, `[\ \]` white brackets.
    91	- Slide 20 — Similarities: traits + multiple inheritance, overloading,
    92	  parametric polymorphism, expression-based, tuples, functional collections
    93	  (map/fold/reduce/filter/sorted/zip), growability, Unicode operators ("But
    94	  Fortress actually uses them!"), strong Haskell influence.
    95	- Slide 21 — Differences: **types are never erased**; fully symmetric dynamic
    96	  overload dispatch (type parameters sometimes inferred at run time); implicit
    97	  as well as explicit parallelism (tuples, binary operands, call arguments);
    98	  whiteboard-driven syntax (∪ ∩ ⊆ ∈, |a|, ⌊x⌋, ⌈x⌉, p∧q...; multiplication as
    99	  `a·b`, `a×b`, or juxtaposition `a b`).
   100	
   101	## 22–33. Syntax: whitespace, juxtaposition, precedence, comprehensions
   102	
   103	- Slides 23–26 — FORTRAN whitespace cautionary tale: `DO 20 I=1,125` (loop) vs
   104	  `DO20I=1.125` (assignment to variable DO20I) vs `DO 20 I=1.125` (also an
   105	  assignment!).
   106	- Slide 27 — Three uses of whitespace in Fortress: disambiguating vertical bars
   107	  `{ |a| | a <- mylist, a | b }`; subscripting `a[i,j,k]` vs `a [i,j,k]`
   108	  (reference then array constructor); *verifying intent of operator precedence*:
   109	  `a+b·c+d` OK, `a + b·c + d` OK, `a+b · c+d` **rejected**.
   110	- Slide 28 — **Juxtaposition is a user-defined overloaded operator** (function
   111	  application and multiplication): `3 sin pi x - log x + 5 z^2 - 7 z + 2`;
   112	  smart string concatenation `"I found" (n+1) "errors in" j "files"`; tight
   113	  juxtaposition binds tighter than loose: `"I generated" n(n-1) "ordered
   114	  pairs"`. Downside: operators must be distinguishable tokens (`MAX`, `MIN`
   115	  uppercase). Scala contrast: any name infix/postfix, but no prefix operators
   116	  beyond `+ - ! ~`. **[repo]** Verified empirically in the chat session:
   117	  `opr juxtaposition` is real; `MultiplicativeRing` default wires jux→TIMES.
   118	- Slide 29 — **Nontransitive operator precedence**: `a+b > c+d` OK; `p<0 ∨ p>9`
   119	  OK; `a+b ∨ c+d` NOT OK — no precedence defined between + and ∨. "We use only
   120	  the most obvious and familiar rules"; matters with hundreds of operator
   121	  symbols; just parenthesize.
   122	- Slide 30 — Binding `x = h+1` ("we see this on whiteboards!") vs mutable
   123	  declaration `y:ZZ := h+1` (type required); assignment is `:=`; compound
   124	  `y += 1`; goal: "mostly pure, SSA" style with a one-character tax.
   125	- Slide 31 — Comments support wiki syntax (superset of Wiki Creole 1.0);
   126	  single backquotes embed Fortress code, rendered typeset.
   127	- Slide 32 — Comprehensions (Haskell notation) for arrays `[...]`, lists
   128	  `<|...|>`, sets `{...}`, multisets `{|...|}` — with typeset equivalents.
   129	- Slide 33 — **Big reduction operators** = fold × comprehension:
   130	  `BIG SUM [p <- mylist, prime p] p+1`, `BIG MAX [k <- 1:n] a[k]`,
   131	  `BIG OPLUS [j <- 1:n, k <- j:n] f(j,k)`. "Reduction operators are exactly
   132	  like comprehensions... Implementationally they are identical."
   133	  **[repo]** `BIG //` / `BIG ||` used in mandelbrot_canonical.fss.
   134	
   135	## 34–37. Parallelism machinery
   136	
   137	- Slide 34 — The ∑ desugaring, all in library code:
   138	  `∑[i<-0:9] a_i x^i` desugars to `∑(0:9, fn i => a_i x^i)`;
   139	  `opr ∑[\E, T extends Monoid[\T,+\]\](g: Generator[\E\], body: E->T): T =
   140	  g.generate(SumReduction[\T\], body)`;
   141	  `object SumReduction[\T extends Monoid[\T,+\]\] extends Reduction[\T\]` with
   142	  `empty(): T = cast[\T\] 0` and `join(a:T,b:T): T = a+b`. ∑ can be overloaded.
   143	  **[repo]** `Monoid[\T,opr\]` DID ship — exactly enough for ∑ (chat-session
   144	  audit).
   145	- Slide 35 — Generators/reducers generic in element type; lazily composable
   146	  (cross product, catenation); algebraic properties encoded in the type system;
   147	  generator controls sequential/parallel strategy; overload dispatch selects
   148	  best reducer per generator; **all defined by library code, not the compiler**.
   149	- Slide 36 — Low-level cooperative parallelism: tuples, arguments, binary
   150	  operators are the real basis; compiler decides which subexpressions become
   151	  microtasks (research area); work-stealing load balancing; "Goal: do for
   152	  processors what GC does for memory."
   153	- Slide 37 — Competitive parallelism: global shared memory; `atomic do ... end`
   154	  appears to execute all at once, implemented with transactional memory;
   155	  nesting with exceptions is "interesting".
   156	
   157	## 38–44. The type system, and where it broke
   158	
   159	- Slide 38 — Hand-drawn hierarchy: Any → {String, Boolean, Number}; Number →
   160	  {Integral → ZZ32, ZZ64, ZZ; Float → RR32, RR64}. Will overloading work with
   161	  `print(x: ...)` for each?
   162	- Slide 39 — How to say you DON'T want sharing (needed for the meet rule /
   163	  overload safety): `excludes` clauses — `trait Boolean extends {Any} excludes
   164	  {String}`, `trait Number ... excludes {String, Boolean}` — **quadratic
   165	  blow-up!**
   166	- Slide 40 — Fix: `partitioned trait Primitive extends {Any}` — children of a
   167	  partitioned trait are pairwise disjoint; hierarchy becomes Any → Primitive →
   168	  {String, Boolean, Number(partitioned)}. **[repo]** `partitioned` never
   169	  shipped; the implementation uses `comprises` + `excludes` (numeric lattice
   170	  ZZ32 <: ZZ64 <: ZZ <: QQ <: RR64 extracted from source in the chat session;
   171	  `Number comprises {RR64}` seals the tower).
   172	- Slide 41 — Fully symmetric dynamic multimethod dispatch on run-time types of
   173	  ALL arguments (no visitor pattern); types never erased: dispatch can tell
   174	  `List[\Boolean\]` from `List[\String\]`, both more specific than `List[\T\]`.
   175	- Slide 42 — Run-time type inference: `crunch(myList)` where
   176	  `myList: List[\Object\] =` a list of threads must infer `T = Thread` at run
   177	  time.
   178	- Slide 43 — Static parameters with interdependent bounds:
   179	  `mangle[\M extends {PartialOrder[\M\], Group[\M,+\]}, F extends M->N,
   180	  N extends List[\M\]\](x:M, f:F): N` — "In general, this requires solving a
   181	  system of type inequalities at run time."
   182	- Slide 44 — **Where We Got Stuck**: generic methods × symmetry requirement →
   183	  parametric meet rule and return type rule → nontrivial run-time constraint
   184	  solving — "'Non-trivial' is a euphemism for 'exponential cost'";
   185	  "Contravariance and union types interact badly"; mitigated by imposing a
   186	  lexical asymmetry on method type parameters; "another nasty case popped up:
   187	  the return type rule has nontrivial consequences." **"So we had a grand
   188	  vision, but could not quite pull it off."**
   189	  **[repo]** This is precisely the subject of the trunk's final commits —
   190	  karl.naden's `Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/` (incl. "rtr algorithm",
   191	  "using constraints", RTRinstantionTheory.tex) and
   192	  `Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`, preserved in the graft.
   193	  [Correction 2026-09-23: these files are in the java.net trunk tip `a874948ac` itself (`justificationOfRTR.tex` from `8015b17f4`, 2012-08-31), not preserved by the graft; see `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.]
   194	
   195	## 45–49. Lessons and reflections
   196	
   197	- Slide 45 — **We learned some good things**: generic types with multiple
   198	  inheritance of generic methods and symmetric dispatch; parallelism with
   199	  automatic work-stealing; factoring parallelism on collections via generators
   200	  and reducers; parsing AND pretty-printing mathematical syntax; nontransitive
   201	  precedence; physical dimensions/units inside a generic type system. "My
   202	  current thinking is to back off and try to exploit a subset of these ideas
   203	  using a less complex type system."
   204	- Slide 46 — Syntax tradeoffs: math notation designed for concision, not
   205	  robustness; juxtaposition made programmable — "sometimes this worked
   206	  beautifully, sometimes it required some weird contortions"; Haskell and Scala
   207	  each capture a PART of mathematical tradition more consistently.
   208	- Slide 47 — Reflections: **"I knew when I started the Fortress project in
   209	  2003..."** (confirms the 2003 start; git history begins 2007-01-04,
   210	  mid-project). Long shot vs Fortran/Java; "we are too often fearful of
   211	  correcting mistakes"; JavaScript aside ("maybe Worse Is Better").
   212	- Slide 48 — Language life cycles: good ideas survive by hopping between
   213	  languages; "the language that develops an idea may not be the one that
   214	  survives"; "I believe in studying history." Fortress → **Swift optional
   215	  binding**: `if x <- z then f(x) else y end` where `z: Maybe[\T\]`.
   216	- Slide 49 — Closer: Greenspun's Tenth Rule.
   217	
   218	## Recovery provenance (for re-download)
   219	
   220	- Wayback direct (id_ = raw bytes), identical digest across ~100 captures
   221	  2021–2026:
   222	  `https://web.archive.org/web/20260416152624id_/https://labs.oracle.com/pls/apex/f?p=LABS:0:100315543614648:APPLICATION_PROCESS=GETDOC_INLINE:::DOC_ID:952`
   223	- Fallback (earliest capture, 2021-12-09):

   227	  the PDF must be dropped into the session by Pavol.

1	# The Fortress project websites, recovered from the Wayback Machine
     2	
     3	Working notes from a 2026-08-21 archive sweep of the project's public web
     4	presence (`projectfortress.sun.com`, the java.net successor, the Oracle
     5	blogs, and the Sun Labs PLRG pages). All quotations below are brief
     6	attributed excerpts from archived pages; every snapshot URL was verified
     7	against the `archive.org/wayback/available` API at sweep time.
     8	
     9	Method note: direct `web.archive.org` page fetches are blocked from the
    10	revival's cloud containers (the availability API works); pages were pulled
    11	through the pure.md reader relay using URLs of the form
    12	`https://pure.md/https://web.archive.org/web/<ts>if_/<encoded-url>`
    13	(the `if_` suffix or `%3A%2F%2F`-encoded target is required; plain forms
    14	404).
    15	
    16	## How the project pitched itself
    17	
    18	Sun-era Trac front page, "Welcome to Project Fortress"
    19	([snapshot 2011-01-25](http://web.archive.org/web/20110125025540/http://projectfortress.sun.com/Projects/Community/)):
    20	
    21	> "Fortress is a new programming language designed for high-performance
    22	> computing (HPC) with high programmability. Fortress features include:
    23	> Implicit parallelism; Transactions; Flexible, space-aware, mathematical
    24	> syntax; Static type-checking (but with type inference); Definition of
    25	> large parts of the language in its own libraries."
    26	
    27	Same page: "The current implementation of Fortress is a reference
    28	interpreter... released under a BSD License... The Sun Labs team is now
    29	hard at work on a compiler."
    30	
    31	The Oracle-era blog masthead carried the best short tagline the sweep
    32	found: **"Project Fortress — Simple parallelism, beautiful code."**
    33	
    34	java.net project blurb
    35	([snapshot 2011-04-11](http://web.archive.org/web/20110411235320/http://java.net/projects/projectfortress)):
    36	"Fortress is a programming language combining easy access to parallelism,
    37	extensibility, static checking and inference, and an uncluttered syntax."
    38	Project tags: `fortress, programming, language, parallelism,
    39	work-stealing`. Started March 2011, owned by dr2chase (David Chase), BSD,
    40	13 members (54 by 2016).
    41	
    42	The famous "do for Fortran what Java did for C" line does **not** appear
    43	on the archived project pages themselves — it is attested in press
    44	coverage (e.g. HPCwire, JavaOne 2008 reports), so cite it as Sun press
    45	framing, not as the site's own words.
    46	
    47	Sun Labs PLRG page
    48	([snapshot 2009-07-18](http://web.archive.org/web/20090718134912/http://research.sun.com/projects/plrg/)):
    49	"Sun Labs Programming Language Research Group", principal investigators
    50	**Guy L. Steele Jr. and Eric Allen**.
    51	
    52	## The specification version ladder — whimsical numbers confirmed
    53	
    54	The PLRG publications page
    55	([snapshot 2008-03-18](http://web.archive.org/web/20080318151108/http://research.sun.com/projects/plrg/Publications/))
    56	lists the pre-1.0 spec versions: **0.618, 0.707, 0.785, 0.866, 0.903,
    57	0.954, 1.0α, 1.0β** (authors Allen, Chase, Hallett, Luchangco, Maessen,
    58	Ryu, Steele, Tobin-Hochstadt). The first four are recognizable constants
    59	converging on 1.0 — 1/φ, √2/2, π/4, √3/2 — the identities of 0.903 and
    60	0.954 are unconfirmed (log₁₀8 ≈ 0.903 and log₁₀9 ≈ 0.954 fit numerically).
    61	
    62	Archived draft PDFs verified in the Wayback Machine:
    63	
    64	- [fortress0618.pdf](https://web.archive.org/web/20080516114706/http://research.sun.com/projects/plrg/fortress0618.pdf)
    65	- [fortress0707.pdf](https://web.archive.org/web/20080509190649/http://research.sun.com/projects/plrg/fortress0707.pdf)
    66	- [fortress0866.pdf](https://web.archive.org/web/20070221211409/http://research.sun.com/projects/plrg/fortress0866.pdf)
    67	- the evolving `fortress.pdf`, earliest capture 2006-12-08
    68	- the final 1.0 spec, later served from
    69	  [labs.oracle.com](https://web.archive.org/web/20130120063452/http://labs.oracle.com/projects/plrg/Publications/fortress.1.0.pdf)
    70	
    71	(The 1.0 title page in this repo's `Specification-1.0-frozen/` says
    72	**March 31, 2008**; Springer's *Encyclopedia of Parallel Computing* entry
    73	says April 2008 — the title page is authoritative. Spec co-author Sam
    74	Tobin-Hochstadt independently hosts a byte-identical copy of the 1.0 PDF
    75	at https://samth.github.io/fortress-spec.pdf — SHA-256 `06f3a627…`
    76	matches ours; verified 2026-08-21.)
    77	
    78	Items from the publications list beyond the usual citations:
    79	
    80	- Hallett, *Semantics and Type Soundness Proof of a Core Fragment of
    81	  Fortress with Hidden Type Variables*.
    82	- Allen, Hallett, Luchangco, Ryu, Tobin-Hochstadt, *Ensuring Acyclicity
    83	  of the Type Hierarchy in Core Fortress*.
    84	- Tobin-Hochstadt, Allen, *A Core Calculus of Metaclasses* (FOOL 2005)
    85	  and *Formal Semantics for MCJ*.
    86	- Allen, Chase, Flood, Luchangco, Maessen, Ryu, Steele, *"Project
    87	  Fortress: A Multicore Language for Multicore Processors"*, Linux
    88	  Magazine, September 2007.
    89	- Talks 2004–2007: Steele's *A Growable Language* (OOPSLA 2006, 90 min),
    90	  *The Soul of a New Programming Language* (JAOO 2006), *Parallel
    91	  Programming and Parallel Abstractions in Fortress* (PACT 2005, FLOPS
    92	  2006, university/industry tour), PLDI 2006 tutorial (Maessen & Steele),
    93	  Chase's *Fortress 0.62* (PPoPP 2005), Allen's FOOL/WOOD 2007 invited
    94	  talk.
    95	
    96	## The wind-down announcement (July 2012)
    97	
    98	**"Fortress Wrapping Up"**, posted by Guy Steele ("gls"), July 20, 2012 —
    99	[snapshot 2012-10-07](https://web.archive.org/web/20121007034544/https://blogs.oracle.com/projectfortress/entry/fortress_wrapping_up);
   100	a [2016 capture](https://web.archive.org/web/20160924201206/https://blogs.oracle.com/projectfortress/entry/fortress_wrapping_up)
   101	additionally preserves 17 reader comments. This post is the entire
   102	announcement — there was no separate wind-down FAQ. Key sentences:
   103	
   104	> "After working nearly a decade on the design, development, and
   105	> implementation of the Fortress programming language, the Oracle Labs
   106	> Programming Language Research Group is now winding down the Fortress
   107	> project. Ten years is a remarkably long run for an industrial research
   108	> project (one to three years is much more typical)..."
   109	
   110	> "...we encountered some severe technical challenges having to do with
   111	> the mismatch between the (rather ambitious) Fortress type system and a
   112	> virtual machine not designed to support it (that would be every
   113	> currently available VM, not just JVM)."
   114	
   115	> "The Fortress source code remains open-source, and the code repository
   116	> will remain available for the foreseeable future."
   117	
   118	The post credits Chapel, X10, Clojure, and Scala as "friendly
   119	competition", lists **eight aspects "we are quite pleased with"**
   120	(generators/reducers; work-stealing implicit parallelism; nested atomic
   121	blocks on transactional memory; non-erased parametric polymorphism;
   122	symmetric multimethod dispatch; symmetric multiple inheritance with type
   123	exclusion; mathematical syntax and juxtaposition; components and APIs)
   124	and **three "wish we had explored further"** (dimensions and units;
   125	explicit data distribution / processor assignment; conditional
   126	inheritance via `where` clauses). Press echo: SD Times, *"Fortress
   127	Finally Folds"*, July 24, 2012.
   128	
   129	## Community and site mechanics
   130	
   131	- Trac-based site with open registration; tickets doubled as
   132	  language-change proposals; anonymous SVN
   133	  (`svn checkout https://projectfortress.sun.com/svn/Community/trunk PFC`);
   134	  contributions required a faxed Sun Contributor Agreement. "Project
   135	  Fortress is led by the Programming Language Research Group of Sun
   136	  Microsystems Labs. Our work was originally funded by the DARPA HPCS
   137	  project, and has continued as a Sun Labs project."
   138	- Front-page timeline (from the 2011-01-25 capture): Jan 2009 Java 1.6
   139	  required; May 2009 MIT tutorial + reference card; Jun 2009 "fortifier"
   140	  web service (Fortress source → rendered PDF); Oct 2009 Trac blog;
   141	  **May 12, 2010: "Sun Labs is now part of Oracle. The Fortress project
   142	  continues as before"**; a 2009-11-16 pre-compiled zip of "an updated
   143	  version of Fortress 1.0" including "the first work towards a compiler".
   144	- March 2011: migration Trac → java.net, SVN → **Mercurial**
   145	  ([snapshot](http://web.archive.org/web/20110411185649/http://projectfortress.java.net/)).
   146	  Compiler status there: the bytecode optimizer had brought compiled-code
   147	  performance "to about 4x Java timings" on the test benchmark; RTTI for
   148	  generic overload dispatch and covariant types ("necessary for the
   149	  'right' implementation of the numeric hierarchy") in progress.
   150	- Mailing lists (announce, builds, commits, dev, issues, users
   151	  @projectfortress.java.net; admins dr2chase, Guy Steele, chmf, victorl,
   152	  tristan) —
   153	  [snapshot 2016-10-17](https://web.archive.org/web/20161017175624/https://java.net/projects/projectfortress/lists).
   154	  No archives of the Sun-era list contents were found anywhere (open
   155	  hunt).
   156	- Learning resources named on the site: the Project Fortress
   157	  [Reference Card](https://web.archive.org/web/20160304052722/https://java.net/downloads/projectfortress/reference.pdf),
   158	  a Quick Vocabulary Guide, intern "Boot Camp" materials, "Fortress by
   159	  Example".
   160	- Two blogs: the Trac blog, Oct 2009 – Jun 2010
   161	  ([snapshot](http://web.archive.org/web/20091109201341/http://projectfortress.sun.com/Projects/Community/blog);
   162	  technical posts: treaps compile, conditional-expression/coercion rules,
   163	  tables and graphics in rendered comments) and the Oracle blog,
   164	  2011–2012, only five posts ending in "Wrapping Up"
   165	  ([index](https://web.archive.org/web/20160422034012/https://blogs.oracle.com/projectfortress/)).
   166	
   167	Other verified snapshots worth keeping:
   168	
   169	- Earliest whole-site capture:
   170	  [2009-01-30](http://web.archive.org/web/20090130012650/http://projectfortress.sun.com/)
   171	- sunsource-era page:
   172	  [2009-03-08](http://web.archive.org/web/20090308082810/http://fortress.sunsource.net/)
   173	- Trac timeline (Wikipedia's "Active Timeline" external link):
   174	  [2011-07-16](http://web.archive.org/web/20110716163020/http://projectfortress.sun.com/Projects/Community/timeline)
   175	- Oracle Labs PLRG:
   176	  [2013-01-15](http://web.archive.org/web/20130115202843/http://labs.oracle.com/projects/plrg/)
   177	- HPCS-exit context (Nov 2006), Simon Phipps' blog:
   178	  [2012-01-06 capture](http://web.archive.org/web/20120106124629/http://blogs.oracle.com/simons/entry/sun_not_selected_for_hpcs)
   179	- Steele's Cornell colloquium abstract, Jan 2008 (still live:
   180	  https://www.cs.cornell.edu/colloquium/2008sp/steele.htm): "While the
   181	  language design was originally aimed at high-end ('petascale') parallel
   182	  supercomputers, it appears also to be well-suited for programming
   183	  multicore chip and multicore cluster systems."
   184	- Lambda the Ultimate wind-down thread (preserves the type-system quote):
   185	  https://lambda-the-ultimate.org/node/4570
   186	
   187	## Dead ends (2026-08-21, from the cloud container)
   188	
   189	arquivo.pt has zero captures of projectfortress.sun.com. Sun-era
   190	mailing-list archives: not found (download.oracle.com/javaee-archive
   191	covers Java EE only). No Wayback captures of the "Previous announcements"

1	# Extract: Guy L. Steele Jr., "Four Solutions to a Trivial Problem" (Google TechTalks 2015)
     2	
     3	> **DRAFT — captions-only extract.** This is based solely on the human-made
     4	> YouTube captions of the talk. The slides — full of charts, diagrams, and
     5	> Fortress code in mathematical notation — were **not** available (no slide
     6	> PDF has been found on the open web; see `research/README.md` for the
     7	> recovery routes), so all slide content described below is inferred from
     8	> what Steele says. Obvious transcription artifacts in the captions
     9	> (garbled notation, lowercased "Fortress", split-up words) have been
    10	> corrected in the quotations below; paraphrase stays outside quotation
    11	> marks. A proper transcript aligned with reconstructed slides (frame
    12	> extraction from the video) is planned, will be cleaned the same way,
    13	> and will supersede this draft.
    14	
    15	- **Title:** Four Solutions to a Trivial Problem
    16	- **Speaker:** Guy L. Steele Jr. (Oracle Labs)
    17	- **Venue:** Google TechTalks (talk given at a Google office; introduced by "Matt")
    18	- **Date given:** 2015-12-01; **uploaded to YouTube:** 2016-01-28
    19	- **Duration:** 1:01:47
    20	- **Video:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ftcIcn8AmSY
    21	
    22	Extract made 2026-08-22 from the full captions. Timestamps are approximate
    23	(caption cue times). Cross-references to the palimondo/fortress repo state
    24	are marked **[repo]**. This is one of Steele's two retrospective-era talks;
    25	the other is the JuliaCon 2016 keynote (`SteeleJuliaCon2016-extract.md`),
    26	whose slides 4–9 reproduce this talk's toy problem and cite this talk by
    27	name. Where JuliaCon compresses the parallelism story to a few slides, this
    28	talk develops it for a full hour.
    29	
    30	## Thesis [0:55–2:25]
    31	
    32	"The best way to write parallel applications is, as much as possible, not to
    33	have to think about the parallelism" [1:10]. The real issue is
    34	*independence of computation*, which today's languages can't express. His
    35	"over-simplified slogan" [1:51]: "accumulators are bad. Divide and conquer
    36	is good." And: algebraic properties are important — programmers should be
    37	aware of them and communicate them to the compiler. This is the same thesis
    38	as his ICFP 2009 keynote "foldl and foldr Considered Slightly Harmful" and
    39	Strange Loop 2010 "How to Think about Parallel Programming: Not!" (both in
    40	the adjacent canon list in `research/README.md`), here developed with a
    41	worked four-solution example.
    42	
    43	## Warm-up 1: summing a million numbers [2:25–5:30]
    44	
    45	A Fortran DO loop summing an array (he first "forgets" to initialize SUM —
    46	"a very common bug"). The loop's semantics are inherently sequential: its
    47	computation tree has a long left-linear spine. "Fran Allen won a Turing
    48	Award for devoting her life to writing compilers that can undo code like
    49	this, and turn it into code that a parallel computer can really run"
    50	[2:47]. A mathematician instead writes Σ — like Fortran 90's SUM intrinsic,
    51	it "says what to do... but doesn't tell you how, so there's no commitment
    52	yet as to strategy" [3:14]. Marking the DO parallel gives race conditions;
    53	adding atomic makes it correct but sequential again. What you want is the
    54	balanced pairwise tree: log-depth given enough processors.
    55	
    56	## Warm-up 2: length of a Lisp list [5:30–8:30]
    57	
    58	Linear-linked lists force a linear algorithm: "data can dictate the way code
    59	works", and linearly-linked lists are "inherently sequential" [6:40].
    60	Analogy to Peano arithmetic vs. binary numbers [6:48]: unary representation
    61	is the list; positional binary gives log-size representation and (with carry
    62	look-ahead) log-log addition. Then Haskell code for list length with a
    63	*three-way* decomposition — empty / singleton / concatenation of two parts
    64	`a ++ b` — where the code does not say *how* to split; if splits are
    65	balanced and cheap, delay is Θ(log n). Multiway decomposition is the key
    66	paradigm shift.
    67	
    68	## The trivial problem [8:30–11:15]
    69	
    70	An array of integers read as a bar chart; pour water over it; how much water
    71	is retained? Credited to Dan Nussbaum and Steve Heller [8:39] (same credit
    72	as JuliaCon slide 4); "it actually may have appeared in some Google
    73	questionnaires for employment — I'm not sure" [8:41]. The example array
    74	(height-16, answer 35) matches the JuliaCon deck's
    75	`2 6 3 5 2 8 1 4 2 2 5 3 5 7 4 1`. Key insight: water above each bar =
    76	(max to the left MIN max to the right) − bar height, so the per-bar
    77	computations are independent — "this gives us a decomposition into
    78	independent pieces" [9:25].
    79	
    80	## Solution 1: sequential sweeps (Fortress) [11:15–13:45]
    81	
    82	Audience-participation reveal that the code on screen is Fortress: "Fortress
    83	is a programming language designed to look kind of like mathematical
    84	pseudocode and to use mathematical notation. But I assure you this is
    85	actually actual, functioning, running code, or at least it was as of three
    86	years ago, last time I checked it" [11:40–11:50]. **[repo]** December 2015
    87	minus three years ≈ late 2012 — i.e. Steele last ran Fortress right around
    88	the July 2012 wind-down announcement and this repo's HEAD (Aug 2012). The
    89	revival's green suite makes his code runnable again.
    90	
    91	The function `histogramWater(x)` does three loops: a left-to-right MAX
    92	accumulation, a right-to-left MAX accumulation, and a final
    93	MIN/subtract/accumulate pass. "I said the nasty word accumulation. This is
    94	going to be a sequential algorithm" [10:14]. An optimizing compiler could
    95	fuse the last two loops into a two-pass version — "that's a difficult thing
    96	for a compiler to do" [13:15].
    97	
    98	## Solution 2: pure divide-and-conquer — bitonic globs [13:45–23:35]
    99	
   100	Recursively split the bar chart, solve halves, merge. The merge abstraction
   101	is a "glob": a *bitonic* outline ("it can go up and then it can go down —
   102	or, as they said of the Monty Python brontosaurus..." [15:10]) plus the
   103	amount of water already inside (just an integer — the shape of the water is
   104	never needed). Representation: list of plateaus (height–width pairs) left of
   105	the peak, the peak's height and width, plateaus right of the peak, and the
   106	water count — five components. Combining two globs has three cases (left
   107	peak higher / right higher / equal); the awkward part is a three-way *split*
   108	of one outline at a given height.
   109	
   110	The Fortress code declares `object GlobReduction extends
   111	MonoidReduction[\Glob\]` [18:42] — "that's essentially a promise that the ⊕ operator, the
   112	combining operator, is going to be associative. That, in turn, will justify
   113	a parallel implementation" [18:45]. Is the complicated ⊕ actually
   114	associative? He has verified it by hand ("It's a pain. It'd be nice to have
   115	a theorem prover do it, or a theorem prover built into a compiler — even
   116	better" [21:25]) — the same theorem-prover wish as JuliaCon slide 15's
   117	`property` laws. **[repo]** `trait Monoid[\T, opr OPLUS\]`
   118	(`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2823`) and `trait MonoidReduction`
   119	(`:2952`, also `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss:414`) are exactly this shipped
   120	machinery; the `BIG` operator desugaring lives in `__bigOperatorSugar` /
   121	`__bigOperator` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1114`).
   122	
   123	Given ⊕, the solution is a one-liner [22:40–23:07]: map every element to a
   124	singleton glob, hit it with big ⊕, extract the water component. "It was
   125	very, very clever to be able to write this solution as a one-liner, once we
   126	built up this very complicated data structure and its associated operations"
   127	[23:10] — the irony is intentional.
   128	
   129	In Q&A [55:40–56:55] he concedes the glob merge is not constant-time: the
   130	three-way split is a binary (log-time) decomposition of the outline list,
   131	so combining is not O(1) and the overall delay is "probably the square of
   132	log n". "I'd love to find a way to do better in this
   133	approach."
   134	
   135	## Solution 3: monoid-cached tree [23:35–29:15]
   136	
   137	Build an explicit in-memory tree over the array whose internal nodes cache
   138	the MAX of their leaves — a "monoid-cached tree", monoid being "a technical
   139	mathematician's term that just means the operation is associative, and that
   140	it has an identity" [23:58]. Fortress code: `trait CachedTree comprises
   141	{NullNode, SingletonNode, PairNode}`; the NullNode holds the identity (−∞
   142	for MAX); construction splits the list into approximately equal pieces with
   143	a comment "parallel recursion here" — "Fortress allows the two expressions
   144	in a tuple expression to be computed independently" [25:35]. **[repo]**
   145	This is the same `maxCachedTree`/`walk` code shown (against a sequential
   146	Scala twin) on JuliaCon slides 18–19; implicit parallelism of tuples and of
   147	binary-operator operands is JuliaCon slide 21/36.
   148	
   149	Then a downward sweep passes information left-child→right-child to compute
   150	the left-to-right MAX sweep in log jumps; mirrored, the *same* tree serves
   151	the right-to-left sweep ("the MAX-cached tree itself is symmetric" [27:00]);
   152	careful coding computes both at once. Two pages of code instead of four or
   153	five, no bespoke glob structure, "and it made use of an abstraction, the
   154	monoid-cached tree, that might actually be useful in other settings"
   155	[29:00] — the beginnings of a library routine.
   156	
   157	## Solution 4: parallel prefix — the true one-liner [29:15–33:20]
   158	
   159	The sweeps are parallel prefix operations (checkbook running-balance
   160	metaphor [29:30]). Abstract them as library operators — MAX with a
   161	left-arrow or right-arrow over it, "a conceptual left-to-right sweep. I'm
   162	not going to see how it's implemented any more than I see how big sigma is
   163	implemented" [30:50]. Then: "Once I have those operators in my library, no
   164	more boilerplate. I have a true one-liner in Fortress here — and this works
   165	in Fortress" [31:20]: zip x with its MAX-prefix and MAX-suffix, and for
   166	each triple `(v, left, right)` sum up `(left MIN right) − v`. This is
   167	exactly the concise solution typeset on JuliaCon slide 9. He names the
   168	structure: "this is a generate step in the yellow, a mapping step... and a
   169	reduce operation, the big sigma. So this is map-reducing math notation. And
   170	I think this is actually a really good way to program, not only in the
   171	large, but also in the small" [33:00] — a pointed remark at Google.
   172	**[repo]** The Library really does ship `opr PREFIX_SUM` and `opr
   173	SUFFIX_SUM` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4480`, `:4485`) — each marked
   174	"`(*) For now, use a sequential implementation`": the interface-without-
   175	commitment the talk advocates, with the parallel implementation left as
   176	future work.
   177	
   178	## The argument: deferring the sequential/parallel decision [33:20–40:30]
   179	
   180	Is the one-liner sequential or parallel? Deliberately unanswered. Inlining
   181	sequential implementations + loop fusion yields the efficient two-pass
   182	sequential solution (he has done the transformation by hand — "this is
   183	about the biggest program I can do it by hand on" [34:20]); inlining
   184	parallel implementations + "deforestation, which I would describe as loop
   185	fusion on trees" [34:55] yields the two-pass parallel solution of the
   186	monoid-cached tree. "This is the main point of the talk... it's possible to
   187	write solutions to problems that don't have a commitment as to whether to
   188	be sequential or parallel" [35:10], with the decision automated at compile
   189	time or run time.
   190	
   191	Accumulation vs. divide-and-conquer, structurally: the accumulator's update
   192	operator has type (solution, input) → solution — *asymmetric*, so its
   193	computation trees are forced linear; superb for one sequential processor
   194	(historical aside [36:20]: CPU registers were called "accumulators" from
   195	Hollerith card machines through the early '70s), and space-efficient. The
   196	merge operator has type (solution, solution) → solution: "Just from its
   197	type signature, you can tell it has the possibility to be associative in a
   198	way that the accumulator combining operation does not. And its
   199	associativity is the key to parallelism" [37:55]. Also: "identifying this
   200	associative combining operator usually lends deeper insight into the
   201	problem" [38:10] — he only saw the monoid-cached tree after first building
   202	the glob machinery.
   203	
   204	The algebra glossary in programmer's terms [39:10–40:00]: associativity —
   205	"the way you group them doesn't matter, and that is the key to
   206	parallelism"; commutativity — order doesn't matter; idempotence —
   207	duplicates don't matter (MAX yes, + no); identity — "this value doesn't
   208	matter"; zero — "the other values don't matter. I'm the king, and I trump
   209	everybody else." Such invariants give the implementation "wiggle room"
   210	[40:12] — the freedom to use parallelism, or not, as resources dictate.
   211	
   212	## Manifesto, then engineering [40:30–45:15]
   213	
   214	"DO loops are so 1950s" [40:59]; linked lists likewise (Lisp, 1950s);
   215	Java-style iterators "still so last millennium" — the iterator API "commits
   216	you to a sequential processing paradigm. As soon as you say, well, first
   217	let's set SUM to zero, you're already hosed" [41:20]. A C/Java for loop is
   218	"probably the worst possible way to say map" [41:35]. This has changed his
   219	own style even for sequential code — to the chorus of critics' voices in his
   220	head (Pixar's "Inside Out" [42:33]) he adds: "are you sure you want an
   221	accumulator? Maybe there's a better way to do this" [42:25].
   222	
   223	Parallel languages are typically "a well-known sequential language, and then
   224	bolting on a couple of parallel features on the side. I think it's possible
   225	to do better. **Fortress was an attempt to do that. I think we achieved
   226	partial success, but I think more needs to be done**" [43:00–43:10] — the
   227	talk's central retrospective verdict on the project. Mindset: don't split a
   228	problem into "the first and the rest"; split into equal pieces and merge;
   229	map inputs to singleton solutions and merge those ("that's usually
   230	trickier" [43:40]).
   231	
   232	Then the backing-off [43:47]: "I have put forward a rather extreme
   233	manifesto... And I'm going to back off slightly. In practice, engineering
   234	needs to be done." Optimizations: special-case singleton leaves; branching
   235	factors larger than 2 — he cites Clojure choosing 64-ary trees (Clojure's
   236	tries are in fact 32-way): "I'm not sure that 64 is the ideal number, but I
   237	know it's way better than two. It's also way better than 10 million"
   238	[44:35]; self-balancing trees (red-black, finger trees);
   239	parallel near the root, sequential at or near the leaves; arrays at the
   240	leaves; dynamic choice between sequential processing and recursive
   241	subdivision when iterating an integer range — "This is something we were
   242	experimenting with in Fortress" [45:14]. **[repo]** That experiment is the
   243	generator/reducer machinery of `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` and the
   244	work-stealing runtime (now on stdlib ForkJoin after the jsr166y retirement
   245	rung).
   246	
   247	## Conclusion: parallelism management as garbage collection [45:15–48:10]
   248	
   249	Linear-decomposition programs are "very hard to parallelize. I repeat,
   250	someone won a Turing Award for writing compilers to do that. It shouldn't be
   251	that hard" [45:28]. Programs organized around independence and
   252	divide-and-conquer can run either way, "with the decisions being made
   253	dynamically according to available resources" [45:50].
   254	
   255	The GC analogy (compare JuliaCon slide 36's "Goal: do for processors what GC
   256	does for memory"): garbage collection also dates to the 1950s, was feared
   257	for decades, went mainstream with Java; we accepted its overheads because
   258	manual management "is so terribly hard" [46:40]. "I argue that the
   259	management of parallelism is very much like garbage collection. It's the
   260	automatic assignment of processors, rather than the automatic assignment of
   261	storage. It's the automatic allocation of code to processors, rather than
   262	data to memory" [46:55–47:08]. Overheads will look daunting, then shrink
   263	without disappearing, as with GC. In a world of wildly varying and
   264	heterogeneous processors (and memories): "I think this is our only hope for
   265	true program portability, and not to have to keep rewriting code every five
   266	years" [47:45].
   267	
   268	## Q&A [48:10–1:01:30] — the retrospective material
   269	
   270	- **Getting the ideas into existing languages** [48:30]: purely functional
   271	  languages are one strategy for independence, "Haskell, I think, is the
   272	  preeminent example"; "we see now map-and-reduce features that are being
   273	  introduced into Java, for example, that were quite explicitly inspired by
   274	  Haskell. And I know that the Java design group at Sun, and then Oracle,
   275	  has kept an eye on the Haskell evolution for about the last 10-15 years"
   276	  [49:04] (i.e. Java 8 streams/lambdas, from the JCP insider). But bolting
   277	  on leaves the old idioms "tempting the programmers" — "The question is,
   278	  how do you get old things to drop off?" [49:40]. Language evolution and
   279	  decay may beat designing from scratch.
   280	- **The odds he gave Fortress** [49:55]: it's really hard to get a
   281	  full-blown language adopted if it's unfamiliar and new, he agrees — "**I
   282	  gave Fortress only, at most, a 20% chance of becoming big and making it.
   283	  And surprise, surprise, it is in the 80%. But I think we learned a few
   284	  things from it.**"
   285	- **The JuliaCon invitation, before the fact** [50:05]: he has "had some
   286	  inquiries recently from a Julia users group wanting to... hear a talk
   287	  about Fortress, hoping it can inform the evolution of Julia, which is a
   288	  language that has gained more traction and is headed in this direction" —
   289	  this is the genesis of the JuliaCon 2016 keynote, seven months before it
   290	  was given. **[repo]** The two talks are a pair: this one is the
   291	  parallelism lesson in depth; JuliaCon is the full design retrospective.
   292	- **Complexity objection** [50:30]: a Googler notes the concise solution
   293	  "took the better part of half an hour to explain... to a roomful of Google
   294	  engineers". Steele's answer [51:15–54:45]: he hasn't *proved* it correct
   295	  ("you flatter me"); unfamiliarity is an education problem — poll: ~15
   296	  hands knew parallel prefix, all knew Σ; he wrote papers on parallel
   297	  primitives in the '80s at Thinking Machines (Connection Machine)
   298	  [52:40]; and the analogy is the structured-programming revolution — the
   299	  1972 ACM national conference go-to debate, in which he took part as a
   300	  student, with Bill Wulf (BLISS: systems programming without go-to)
   301	  [53:25]. "It's a matter of figuring out what are the relevant
   302	  primitives" and building community consensus; parallel primitives could
   303	  cover "90% of the structuring of our code" as if-then-else/while did for
   304	  sequential code [54:00]. "It's a grand vision. It's the result of
   305	  synthesizing 40 years of experience" [54:21].
   306	- **Grammars are left/right-recursive** [54:55]: only because parser
   307	  generators emit sequential parsers; "If your parser generator were going
   308	  to generate a parallel parser, you might write your grammars... in a
   309	  different way. And I speak from experience. I've actually tried those
   310	  experiments" [55:10].
   311	- **A thank-you from the audience** [56:55]: "I have used a lot of the
   312	  things that you have built over the years. And I just wanted to say
   313	  thanks." — "Thank you. That means a lot to me that you found something
   314	  useful."
   315	- **Which languages carry the torch** [57:30]: "Julia and Haskell and
   316	  Clojure are probably the most widely used languages that are
   317	  intentionally exploring in these directions. I think such exploration
   318	  could also be done in say, Scala. But the Scala community, I think, has
   319	  not made a priority of investigating that dimension." On Python [58:10]:
   320	  he'd be delighted, but the exploring fraction is small; Julia's community
   321	  is small "but they are really pressing in this direction. And they're all
   322	  more popular than Fortress, you know? So help me, Obi-Wan, you're my only
   323	  hope" [58:29]. "I'm just going around talking to all kinds of
   324	  communities, including you, hoping to find some interest. And maybe
   325	  you'll take it in a direction I never thought of" [58:40].
   326	- **Inertia of today's larger community** [58:50]: more inertia, but "less
   327	  resistance today to new ideas" than the fractious 1960s–70s ("Fortran is
   328	  good enough for us, thank you — or COBOL"); he sees "a lot less of the
   329	  programming language, religion wars" [1:00:10].
   330	- **UI programming** [1:00:20]: "part of the problem is that our users tend
   331	  to be sequential. If only we had parallel users, then things might be
   332	  easier" [1:00:53]; HTML designed differently would expose more
   333	  independent parts of a page; "I think there's opportunity everywhere" —
   334	  whether to exploit it is engineering.
   335	
   336	## Open items for the slide-aligned redo
   337	
   338	- Reconstruct the slides by frame extraction from the video (route 3 in
   339	  `research/README.md`); align quotes to slide numbers as in the JuliaCon
   340	  extract.
   341	- Recover the exact Fortress code for: the three-loop sequential
   342	  `histogramWater`, the glob object/⊕/split, the CachedTree +
   343	  `process` two-pass sweep, and the prefix/suffix one-liner — then try to
   344	  run them on the revived interpreter. **[repo]** JuliaCon slide 9 gives
   345	  the one-liner's typeset form; the rest exists only in this video.
   346	- Check whether the talk's deck is another Archivist DOC_ID on the Oracle
   347	  Labs APEX host (CDX enumeration, `research/README.md`).

1	# Extract: the Fortress code of "Four Solutions to a Trivial Problem"
     2	
     3	Working notes on the code slides of Guy L. Steele Jr.'s Google TechTalk
     4	(2015-12-01, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ftcIcn8AmSY, slides (c) 2015
     5	Oracle). Transcribed by hand from screenshots of the talk video (supplied
     6	by Pavol, 2026-08-24) back to ASCII Fortress source -- the inverse of what
     7	bin/fortick does. Our own transcription and commentary; per repo policy no
     8	slide images are committed. Companion to
     9	SteeleGoogleTechTalk2015-extract.md (the captions-only content extract,
    10	which carries the timestamps).
    11	
    12	Purpose: best-practice grounding for the microgpt canonical-form rewrite
    13	-- see explorations/microgpt-native-brief.md.
    14	
    15	Transcription conventions: subscripts `left_k` are array indexing
    16	`left[k]`, white brackets are `[\ \]`, angle lists are `<| |>`, Sigma
    17	with a generator under it is `SUM[gen]`, oplus is `OPLUS`, parallel-bars
    18	concatenation is `||`. Verification: feed these back through fortick and
    19	compare the render to the screenshots.
    20	
    21	## s1-sequential.jpg — "Sequential Code" (Solution 1)
    22	
    23	```fortress
    24	histogramWater(x: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]): ZZ32 = do
    25	  n = |x|
    26	  if n = 0 then 0 else
    27	    left = array[\ZZ32\](n)
    28	    left[0] := x[0]
    29	    for k <- seq(1 : n-1) do left[k] := left[k-1] MAX x[k] end
    30	    right = array[\ZZ32\](n)
    31	    right[n-1] := x[n-1]
    32	    for k <- seq(n-2 : 0 : -1) do right[k] := right[k+1] MAX x[k] end
    33	    result: ZZ32 := 0
    34	    for k <- seq(0 : n-1) do result += ((left[k] MIN right[k]) - x[k]) end
    35	    result
    36	  end
    37	end
    38	```
    39	
    40	Idioms: strided range `seq(n-2:0:-1)`; compound assignment `+=`;
    41	`array[\T\](n)` allocation; `|x|` for size; if-expression returns value.
    42	
    43	## s1-sequential-optimized.jpg — "Sequential Code (Optimized)"
    44	
    45	```fortress
    46	histogramWater(x: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]): ZZ32 = do
    47	  n = |x|
    48	  if n = 0 then 0 else
    49	    left = array[\ZZ32\](n)
    50	    left[0] := x[0]
    51	    for k <- seq(1 : n-1) do left[k] := left[k-1] MAX x[k] end
    52	    right: ZZ32 := x[n-1]
    53	    result: ZZ32 := 0
    54	    for k <- seq(n-1 : 0 : -1) do
    55	      right MAX= x[k]
    56	      result += ((left[k] MIN right) - x[k])
    57	    end
    58	    result
    59	  end
    60	end
    61	```
    62	
    63	Idioms: compound operator assignment `MAX=` — ANY operator can compound-
    64	assign. The two-pass fused form (the one our microgpt "would compile to").
    65	
    66	## s2-glob-structure.jpg — "Glob Data Structure and Utility Operations"
    67	
    68	```fortress
    69	object Glob(left: List[\(ZZ32,ZZ32)\], ht: ZZ32, wd: ZZ32,
    70	            right: List[\(ZZ32,ZZ32)\], water: ZZ32)
    71	end
    72	
    73	width(x: List[\(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]) = SUM[(p,q) <- x] q
    74	
    75	fill(x: List[\(ZZ32,ZZ32)\], m: ZZ32) = SUM[(p,q) <- x] q (m - p)
    76	
    77	object GlobReduction
    78	        extends { MonoidReduction[\Glob\],
    79	                  ReductionWithZeroes[\Glob, Glob\] }
    80	    getter asString(): String = "GlobReduction"
    81	    empty(): Glob = Glob(<| |>, -INFINITY, 0, <| |>, 0)
    82	    join(a: Glob, b: Glob): Glob = a OPLUS b
    83	end
    84	
    85	opr BIG OPLUS(): BigReduction[\Glob, Glob\] = BigReduction[\Glob, Glob\](GlobReduction)
    86	```
    87	
    88	THE key slide. Idioms: `SUM[(p,q) <- x] q` — big-operator comprehension
    89	with tuple-destructuring generator, one line per mathematical definition.
    90	User-defined reduction: object extending MonoidReduction[\T\] with
    91	empty()/join(); then `opr BIG OPLUS()` registers a user-defined BIG
    92	operator usable as `BIG OPLUS [g <- gen] expr`. (Note slide shows q×(m−p)
    93	with explicit ×; juxtaposition also fine.) `-INFINITY` as monoid identity.
    94	
    95	## s2-threewaysplit.jpg — "Utility Operation for Splitting Sorted Lists"
    96	
    97	```fortress
    98	threeWaySplit(x: List[\(ZZ32,ZZ32)\], m: ZZ32): (List[\(ZZ32,ZZ32)\], Maybe[\ZZ32\], List[\(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]) =
    99	  if |x| = 0 then (<| |>, Nothing, <| |>)
   100	  elif |x| = 1 then
   101	    (a, b) = x[0]
   102	    if a < m then (x, Nothing, <| |>)
   103	    elif a > m then (<| |>, Nothing, x)
   104	    else (<| |>, Just b, <| |>) end
   105	  else
   106	    (y, z) = x.split()   (* into approximately equal nonempty pieces *)
   107	    (n, w) = z[0]
   108	    if m < n then
   109	      (p, q, r) = threeWaySplit(y, m)
   110	      (p, q, r || z)
   111	    else
   112	      (p, q, r) = threeWaySplit(z, m)
   113	      (y || p, q, r)
   114	    end
   115	  end
   116	```
   117	
   118	Idioms: `x.split()` — the List's own parallel-decomposition primitive
   119	(this is what makes List a generator that divides); tuple returns and
   120	tuple destructuring everywhere; Maybe/Nothing/Just; `||` concatenation.
   121	
   122	## s2-oplus-combiner.jpg — "Code for Combining Two Bitonic Globs"
   123	
   124	```fortress
   125	opr OPLUS(x: Glob, y: Glob): Glob =
   126	  case (x.ht CMP y.ht) of
   127	    LessThan =>
   128	      (lss, eql, gtr) = threeWaySplit(y.left, x.ht)
   129	      Glob(x.left || <| (x.ht, x.wd + width(x.right) + width(lss) + eql.getDefault(0)) |> || gtr,
   130	           y.ht, y.wd, y.right,
   131	           x.water + fill(x.right, x.ht) + fill(lss, x.ht) + y.water)
   132	    GreaterThan =>
   133	      (lss, eql, gtr) = threeWaySplit(x.right, y.ht)
   134	      Glob(x.left, x.ht, x.wd,
   135	           y.right || <| (y.ht, eql.getDefault(0) + width(lss) + width(y.left) + y.wd) |> || gtr,
   136	           x.water + fill(lss, y.ht) + fill(y.left, y.ht) + y.water)
   137	    EqualTo =>
   138	      Glob(x.left, x.ht, x.wd + width(x.right) + width(y.left) + y.wd, y.right,
   139	           x.water + fill(x.right, x.ht) + fill(y.left, x.ht) + y.water)
   140	  end
   141	```
   142	
   143	Idioms: user `opr OPLUS` on a user object; `case (a CMP b) of LessThan/
   144	GreaterThan/EqualTo` three-way comparison dispatch; the slide's punchline
   145	"Is it associative?" — the operator is engineered to BE associative so
   146	the BIG reduction may regroup freely: associativity as a designed,
   147	load-bearing property, not an accident.
   148	
   149	
   150	## s2-final-oneliner.jpg — "Final Divide-and-Conquer Code" (slide 59)
   151	
   152	```fortress
   153	histogramWater(x: List[\ZZ32\]): ZZ32 = (BIG OPLUS[v <- x] Glob(<| |>, v, 1, <| |>, 0)).water
   154	```
   155	
   156	The whole of Solution 2's top level: map each element into the monoid
   157	(a singleton Glob), BIG-reduce with the user-defined ⊕, project the
   158	answer. Generate-map-reduce as ONE expression; parallelism implicit in
   159	the reduction tree.
   160	
   161	## s3-cachedtree-adt.jpg — "Code to Make a MAX-cached Tree (1 of 2)" (slide 66)
   162	
   163	```fortress
   164	trait CachedTree comprises { NullNode, SingletonNode, PairNode }
   165	  getter val(): ZZ32
   166	end
   167	
   168	object NullNode(val: ZZ32) extends CachedTree end
   169	object SingletonNode(val: ZZ32) extends CachedTree end
   170	object PairNode(val: ZZ32, a: CachedTree, b: CachedTree) extends CachedTree end
   171	
   172	maxCachedTree(x: List[\ZZ32\]) =
   173	  if |x| = 0 then NullNode(-INFINITY)
   174	  elif |x| = 1 then SingletonNode(x[0])
   175	  else
   176	    (p, q) = x.split()   (* into approximately equal nonempty pieces *)
   177	    (a, b) = (maxCachedTree p, maxCachedTree q)   (* parallel recursion here *)
   178	    PairNode(a.val MAX b.val, a, b)
   179	  end
   180	```
   181	
   182	Idioms: `comprises` — a SEALED sum type (closed algebraic data type) as
   183	a trait; abstract getter in the trait, leaf objects supply it via
   184	constructor params. **THE parallel idiom: `(a, b) = (f p, f q)` — tuple
   185	component evaluation is implicitly parallel.** Steele's own comment
   186	marks it: "parallel recursion here". No task API, no seq/par keyword —
   187	the TUPLE is the fork.
   188	
   189	## s3-process-multimethod.jpg — "Efficient Parallel Solution (Two Passes)"
   190	
   191	```fortress
   192	histogramWater(x: List[\ZZ32\]): ZZ32 = process(maxCachedTree x, -INFINITY, -INFINITY)
   193	
   194	process(x: PairNode, left: ZZ32, right: ZZ32): ZZ32 =
   195	  (* parallel recursion here *)
   196	  process(x.a, left, x.b.val MAX right) + process(x.b, left MAX x.a.val, right)
   197	
   198	process(x: SingletonNode, left: ZZ32, right: ZZ32): ZZ32 =
   199	  ((left MIN right) MAX x.val) - x.val
   200	
   201	process(x: NullNode, left: ZZ32, right: ZZ32): ZZ32 = 0
   202	```
   203	
   204	Idioms: structural recursion by MULTIMETHOD DISPATCH — three `process`
   205	definitions selected by node type; no case/match on the sum type at
   206	all. And again implicit parallelism: the two operands of `+` evaluate
   207	in parallel ("parallel recursion here"). Slide's own footer: "Two pages
   208	of code total, and no need to operate on a special 'glob' data
   209	structure."
   210	
   211	## s4-concise-final.jpg — "Concise Solution (6 of 6)" (slide 83)
   212	
   213	```fortress
   214	histogramWater(x: List[\ZZ32\]): ZZ32 =
   215	  SUM[(v, left, right) <- zip(x, PREFIX_MAX x, SUFFIX_MAX x)] ((left MIN right) - v)
   216	```
   217	
   218	(Typeset: Σ under-annotated with the 3-tuple generator; MAX with over-
   219	arrows = the prefix/suffix scan operators — our arrow-notation fix
   220	renders exactly these.) Slide text: "Inlining and loop fusion transform
   221	this into the efficient two-pass sequential solution. Inlining and
   222	deforestation ('loop fusion on trees') transform this into the
   223	efficient two-pass parallel solution." The one-liner is the SOURCE of
   224	both efficient forms — fold order and pass structure are derived, not
   225	specified.
   226	
   227	## philosophy-algebraic-properties.jpg — "Algebraic Properties Are Important!" (slide 87)
   228	
   229	- Associative: grouping doesn't matter!
   230	- Commutative: order doesn't matter!
   231	- Idempotent: duplicates don't matter!
   232	- Identity: this value doesn't matter!
   233	- Zero: other values don't matter!
   234	
   235	"Invariants give the implementation *wiggle room* — the freedom to
   236	exploit alternate representations and implementations. In particular,
   237	*associativity* gives implementations the necessary wiggle room to use
   238	parallelism — *or not* — as resources dictate."
   239	
   240	The design brief for the microgpt rewrite in five bullets.
   241	
   242	## Philosophy slides (88–91) — the mindset
   243	
   244	**"We Need a New Mindset" (88):** DO loops are so 1950s; so are linear
   245	linked lists; Java-style iterators are so last millennium. **"As soon
   246	as you say 'first, SUM = 0' you are hosed."** "If you say 'process
   247	subproblems in order,' you lose." "A for(;;) loop is the *worst
   248	possible way* to say map." The great tricks of the sequential past
   249	WON'T WORK — but our languages still encourage them.
   250	
   251	**"The Parallel Future" (89):** Top-down: don't split into "the first"
   252	and "the rest" — split into roughly equal pieces, recursively solve,
   253	combine subsolutions. Bottom-up: **don't create a null solution and
   254	successively update it — map inputs independently to singleton
   255	solutions, then merge treewise.** Combining subsolutions is usually
   256	trickier than incremental update (that's where the design work lives —
   257	cf. "Is it associative?").
   258	
   259	**"The Fully Engineered Story" (90):** in practice: optimized singleton
   260	representations; branching factors > 2 (Clojure's 64-ary trees cited);
   261	self-balancing trees (2-3, red-black, finger trees); **use sequential
   262	techniques near the leaves; arrays at the leaves; decide dynamically
   263	whether to process sequentially or by parallel subdivision.** ⇒
   264	Sequential execution belongs at the LEAVES as an engineering layer —
   265	never as the program's semantic shape.
   266	
   267	**"Conclusion" (91):** linear problem decomposition is hard to
   268	parallelize; independence + divide-and-conquer runs parallel OR
   269	sequential as resources dictate; the overheads are real and will
   270	shrink but not disappear (the GC analogy); in a world of parallel
   271	computers of wildly varying sizes *including 1*, this is the only hope
   272	for portability; better language design encourages "independent
   273	thinking."
   274	
   275	(Also replaced s2-threewaysplit.jpg with the full-resolution capture;
   276	transcription re-verified against it — matches.)
